hook.line: When someone says exactly the right thing, English hits a nail on the head, and Spanish does the same, but with a different preposition. Hernando says it whenever a customer finally guesses what Rosa's secret ingredient was.
hook.es: Diste en el clavo con ese regalo.
hook.en: You hit the nail on the head with that present.

examples.es: Diste en el clavo con ese regalo.
examples.en: You hit the nail on the head with that present. (to a friend)

examples.es: La crítica dio en el clavo.
examples.en: The review hit the nail on the head.

examples.es: Dimos en el clavo con el nombre del café.
examples.en: We hit the nail on the head with the name of the café.

examples.es: Mariana dio en el clavo: el problema es el precio.
examples.en: Mariana hit the nail on the head: the problem is the price.

examples.es: No di en el clavo con el menú.
examples.en: I didn't hit the nail on the head with the menu.

examples.es: Usted dio en el clavo, Hernando.
examples.en: You hit the nail on the head, Hernando. (formal)

rule:
*Dar en el clavo* means to get exactly right. *Dar* changes with the person: *di*, *diste*, *dio*, *dimos*, *dieron*. The rest is fixed: *en el clavo*.

Add *con* for what you got right: *dar en el clavo con el nombre*.

To say you missed, use *no*: *No di en el clavo*.

English says "on the head". Spanish just says "in the nail".
smallPrint: Teachers call this an idiom: the meaning is the whole phrase, not the words one by one.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *diste* or *dio* and type the whole sentence, to a friend: *___ en el clavo con ese regalo.*
yourTurn.answer: Diste en el clavo con ese regalo.
yourTurn.why: You are talking to a friend (*tú*), so *diste*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *di* or *dimos* and type the whole sentence, about us: *___ en el clavo con el nombre del café.*
yourTurn.answer: Dimos en el clavo con el nombre del café.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: The review hit the nail on the head.
yourTurn.answer: La crítica dio en el clavo.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I didn't hit the nail on the head with the menu.
yourTurn.answer: No di en el clavo con el menú.
yourTurn.why: *No* goes before *di*, and *con* names what you missed.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to Hernando, formally: You hit the nail on the head, Hernando.
yourTurn.answer: Usted dio en el clavo, Hernando.
yourTurn.why: *Usted* takes the same form as *he* or *she*: *dio*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it about Mariana: *Diste en el clavo.* Type: Mariana hit the nail on the head.
yourTurn.why: The verb changes to match the person, *dio*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Dimos en el clavo con el menú.*
yourTurn.answer: No dimos en el clavo con el menú.

pitfalls.wrong: Diste el clavo en la cabeza.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Spanish has no "head" here, just *dar en el clavo*.

pitfalls.wrong: Diste en el clavo de ese regalo.
pitfalls.right: Diste en el clavo con ese regalo.
pitfalls.why: Almost. What you got right follows *con*.
Almost. The *el* is part of the phrase.

personal: Think of the last time someone said something that was exactly right, and tell them *Diste en el clavo*.
